title: Asynchronous, Generation-Free ABC: Streaming AMIS Reweighting for Heterogeneous Simulator Workloads on HPC
trick: Give each worker a candidate the moment it finishes instead of waiting for the slowest; reweight draws against the mixture of proposals used; the barrier's cost is the expected slowest-of-W runtime over the mean runtime.
framing_stripped: Called 'generation-free ABC with streaming AMIS reweighting'; it is an asynchronous work queue in front of a population sampler (every free worker draws from a Gaussian mixture on the current top-k particles), plus the standard multiple-importance-sampling fix (weight every draw against the average of all proposals ever used, approximated by m <= 21 reconstructed snapshots), plus an order-statistics model of what a lockstep barrier costs.
method_equations: ABC target at bandwidth $\epsilon$ (eq. 1): $\pi_{\epsilon}(\theta \mid y) \propto \pi(\theta) L_{\epsilon}(\theta)$ with $L_{\epsilon}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim p(\rho \mid \theta)}[K_{\epsilon}(\rho)]$, where $\theta$ = parameters, $y$ = observations, $\rho$ = discrepancy between simulated and observed summaries, $\pi$ = prior, $K_{\epsilon}$ = a smooth kernel with $K_{\epsilon}(0) = 1$ (Gaussian or Epanechnikov; the hard indicator is excluded). History at call $n$ (eq. 3): $\mathcal{H}_n = \{(\theta_i, \rho_i, \epsilon_i, w_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$, $\epsilon_i$ = bandwidth in force when $\theta_i$ was proposed, $w_i$ = its parent weight; archive $A_n$ = the $k$ history members with smallest $\rho_i$ ($k = 100$). Bandwidth: nonincreasing; at each search the largest $\epsilon$ retaining $95\%$ of the archive's kernel-weighted effective sample size, at most halved per update, held until $2k$ evaluated particles lie below it (sec. 3.3). Proposal (eq. 4): $q_n(\theta) = \sum_{j \in A_n} \tilde{W}^{(n)}_j K_{\Sigma}(\theta - \theta_j)$ with $\tilde{W}^{(n)}_j \propto w_j K_{\epsilon_n}(\rho_j)$ normalized to one and $\Sigma_n = s \, \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_{\tilde{W}}(A_n)$ (weighted archive covariance scaled by $s$, truncated to the prior box). Parent weight of a new draw (eq. 5): $w^{\star} = \pi(\theta^{\star}) / \bar{q}^{\mathrm{on}}_n(\theta^{\star})$, $\bar{q}^{\mathrm{on}}_n = \frac{1}{1 + |\mathcal{S}|}[q_n + \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} q_s]$, $\mathcal{S}$ = the last $S = 20$ proposal snapshots taken one per $k$ calls. Posterior estimate over the whole history (eqs. 6-7): $\widehat{\pi}_n(f) = \sum_i W_{i,n} f(\theta_i) / \sum_i W_{i,n}$ with $W_{i,n} = \pi(\theta_i) K_{\epsilon_n}(\rho_i) / \bar{q}_n(\theta_i)$ and $\bar{q}_n = \lambda_n \pi + (1 - \lambda_n) \sum_{s=1}^{m} \alpha_{s,n} q_{\tau_s}$, where $q_{\tau_s}$ = proposal rebuilt from the history truncated at index $\tau_s$, $\alpha_{s,n}$ = share of draws that snapshot represents, $\lambda_n = \max(\nu_n, \delta)$ with $\nu_n$ = observed fraction of prior draws and $\delta = 0.5/(m+1)$ a floor that bounds the weights. Fidelity ratio (eq. 8): $r_n = \bar{q}^{\star}_n / \bar{q}_n$ with $\bar{q}^{\star}_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i \le n} \tilde{q}_i$ the true mixture of conditional proposal densities; Theorem 1: $\widehat{\pi}_n(f) - \pi^{r_n}_{\epsilon_n}(f) \to 0$ a.s. on $\{\epsilon_\infty > 0\}$, where $\pi^{\varrho}_{\epsilon}(f) = \int f \pi L_{\epsilon} \varrho / \int \pi L_{\epsilon} \varrho$ is the posterior tilted by $\varrho$; $r \equiv 1$ gives the smooth-ABC posterior. Barrier model (sec. 5.3): with $D_i$ = per-evaluation duration (simulation time plus measured coordination overhead) and $W$ = workers, a lockstep generation takes $\mathbb{E}[\max_{i \le W} D_i]$, so $T_{\mathrm{sync}} = W / \mathbb{E}[\max_{i \le W} D_i]$ and the predicted barrier cost is $T_{\mathrm{async}} / T_{\mathrm{sync}}$, which for i.i.d. uncensored durations reduces to $\mathbb{E}[\max_{i \le W} D_i] / \mathbb{E}[D]$; the expectation is taken by resampling $W$ durations from the asynchronous run's own timing record. Deadline censoring (Prop. 9): $|\widehat{\pi}_n(f) - \widehat{\pi}_{n'}(f)| \le 2 \|f\|_\infty W / (\delta n \overline{W}_n)$, $n'$ = candidates launched, $n$ = completed, $\overline{W}_n$ = mean weight. Matched-budget tolerance: $\epsilon_{(k)}(n)$ = $k$-th smallest discrepancy among the first $n$ completed evaluations.
load_bearing_assumption: That a lockstep generation's duration is the maximum of W independent draws from the same runtime distribution the asynchronous run recorded (Assumption 4 B1: durations conditionally independent given parameters; sec. 5.3), and that the barrier's own latency is negligible against one evaluation. Where either fails the predictor is outside its stated domain: at 0x and 1x straggler slowdown the 0.3 s collective dominates a 4 ms workload, and at 384 Cellular Potts workers contention gives the asynchronous timing sample a tail the synchronized generations never showed (sec. 6.1). For the posterior: that the m <= 21 reconstructed snapshots plus a prior floor track the true mixture of n proposals (fidelity ratio r -> 1); two of its four contributions are measured (0.2-0.5% total variation on five Cellular Potts runs), two only bounded (sec. 4, sec. 8).
weakest_component: The headline numbers come from different places than the mechanism. The 400x barrier penalty is an injected persistent straggler (one of 16 workers delayed 2.0 s on a 0.1 ms simulator, Table 9); on the real Cellular Potts simulator at 50^3 the barrier itself costs only 1.2x (runtime CV 0.05) and 1.9x at 80^3 (CV 0.13-0.23), while the 2.1-2.4x advantage over pyABC is mostly pyABC's fixed per-generation overhead against a 13 s evaluation (sec. 6.1). The 1.2x is read off a utilization ratio because the synchronized variant's simulations also ran 6-36 s against 5.1 s asynchronous, a duration gap the paper declines to attribute (Table 11). The predictor is validated on twelve configurations after three were excluded as outside its domain, with 16-19% errors at the widest spreads where the 60 s budget censors the long runs (sec. 6.1). On inference quality the baseline wins the harder case: on 4-D g-and-k pyABC ends at W_1 = 0.029 to the reference against 0.069, the posterior effective sample size stays at 1.9-3.6 times k (238-296 of 1.3 million particles on the Gaussian mean) and ranges 7 to 2987 across g-and-k checkpoints (sec. 6.4), and below about 4 ms per simulation the all-to-all per-arrival exchange costs more than the barrier it removes (pyABC completes 3.5x more simulations on the 0.1 ms benchmark, sec. 6.3).
regime: ABC parameter inference on CPU simulators over MPI on the JUWELS cluster, 48 cores per node. Five benchmarks (Table 1): Gaussian mean (d = 1, 0.1 ms/sim, 48 workers, 300 s; injected straggler 0-20x on 16 workers; lognormal runtime spread sigma <= 2), g-and-k (d = 4, 2 ms, 600 s), Lotka-Volterra (d = 4, 4 ms, 98% of simulations extinct, scaling 1-288 workers), Cellular Potts tissue model at 50^3 (d = 2, 13 s per evaluation of four replicate simulations, CV 0.05, 3600 s, scaling to 384 workers) and 80^3 (170 s, CV 0.13-0.23, 48 workers). Archive k = 100, snapshots S = 20, five replicates (three at 80^3). Results: predicted-to-measured barrier cost 0.84-1.19 (median 0.996) over twelve configurations spanning 1.2x to 400x; pyABC idles 51-79% under heterogeneity against 1-27%, 43-49% utilization on Cellular Potts against 98-99.8%; 2.1-2.4x the evaluations per hour and 4.1x tighter epsilon_(100) at equal wall clock on Cellular Potts 50^3, 2.1x per-simulation efficiency at 80^3; throughput parity with pyABC at about 4 ms per simulation; 97% parallel efficiency to eight nodes at 13 s per evaluation; calibration nominal in 1-D, conservative on two of four g-and-k parameters; cell-volume contraction 81% +/- 1% against pyABC 72% +/- 4%, ESS 303 against 66.
information_asymmetry: (1) Dispatch vs completion: at dispatch time the scheduler does not know how long an evaluation will take, yet runtime is a function of the parameter (correlation 0.99 between runtime and cell count on Cellular Potts; parameter-coupled runtime in F.5), so the information that would let a scheduler pre-sort or batch by cost exists in the history (every completed evaluation's duration D_i is logged next to its theta_i) and is used by the paper only in hindsight, to predict a counterfactual barrier penalty, never forward to place work. (2) Asynchronous run vs synchronous run: the paper shows the lockstep system's cost can be computed from the asynchronous system's timing log alone (resample W durations, take the expected maximum), so the barrier never has to be built to be priced; the converse is also true and unused, a lockstep run's per-member durations price its own barrier (Table 11 reads it from within-generation max-to-mean ratios). (3) Deadline vs completion: a wall-clock deadline sees only finished evaluations, so cheap parameter regions are over-represented in the sample (length bias, sec. 8); the paper bounds the direct effect at O(W/n) and measures no mean shift on the Gaussian benchmark, but the indirect effect through the adaptive proposal is only covered by the unmeasured part of r. (4) Sampling vs reporting: the scheduler's bandwidth schedule and the archive size k, not the number of simulations, fix the posterior's effective support (ESS at a few multiples of k after 1.3 million draws); the full history exists but the reporting rule discards most of it, and re-reporting a stored history at the k-th order statistic recovers a posterior (93%/85% contraction) with zero new simulations (sec. 6.4). For L5: a batched GPU physics step is this paper's generation with worlds as workers and solver iterations as D_i; each world's iteration count to convergence is known at the end of every step (the solver's residual history) and is as cheap to log as these durations, which is the measurement the lane's scheduler argument needs and no engine reports.
occupies: An asynchronous smooth-kernel ABC sampler with per-arrival top-k Gaussian-mixture proposals and AMIS reweighting of the full history against a bounded number of reconstructed proposal snapshots, its martingale consistency proof (tracking at the realized bandwidth, tilted by a fidelity ratio), the order-statistics prediction of a generation barrier's cost from asynchronous timing alone and its validation across 1.2x-400x, the measured 4 ms crossover below which per-arrival coordination costs more than the barrier, and the Cellular Potts results against a kernel-matched pyABC.

neighbors.title: pyABC: Efficient and robust easy-to-use approximate Bayesian computation
neighbors.trick: A sequential Monte Carlo ABC package that parallelizes the simulations inside each generation across cores and nodes and auto-tunes distances, thresholds and noise handling; it is the generation-based baseline whose barrier this card's paper removes.

neighbors.title: A Wall-time Minimizing Parallelization Strategy for Approximate Bayesian Computation
neighbors.trick: Look-ahead scheduling: workers idle at a generation's end start simulating speculative candidates for the next generation so cores stay busy, giving 10-20% (up to 50%) speed-ups; it keeps the generation, where this card's paper abolishes it.

neighbors.title: Dynamic SBI: Round-free Sequential Simulation-Based Inference with Adaptive Datasets
neighbors.trick: Run simulation and neural posterior training in parallel on a dataset that is continuously filtered and refilled toward the observation, removing the fixed rounds of sequential SBI; the neural counterpart of removing the generation, without an importance-weighted posterior from the simulation log.

neighbors.title: Anytime Monte Carlo
neighbors.trick: Impose a real-time budget instead of a sample count and correct the resulting length bias (samples that take longer are under-represented) with a multiple-chain construction, so all processors are ready for a resampling step together; the deadline-censoring correction this card's paper names as future work.

neighbors.title: Asynchronous Anytime Sequential Monte Carlo
neighbors.trick: The particle cascade: an SMC algorithm with no barrier synchronizations that emits an unbounded particle stream within fixed memory and stays an unbiased marginal-likelihood estimator; barrier-free SMC for state-space models, not ABC and without mixture reweighting.

theme_fit.why: A baseline and a ruler for the lane's scheduler argument, not an answer to it. The paper's generation is a batched GPU physics step: W workers become W worlds stepped in lockstep by one Newton or conjugate-gradient kernel, and the per-evaluation duration D_i becomes world i's solver iteration count N_i to convergence. The lockstep step costs max_i N_i iterations while the useful work is sum_i N_i, so the barrier penalty is E[max_{i <= W} N_i] / E[N], computable from a per-world iteration log alone, exactly the paper's recipe of resampling W durations from the asynchronous record (sec. 5.3), and its calibration is the lane's second kill test (1.2x at runtime CV 0.05, 1.9x at CV 0.13-0.23, 400x with one persistent straggler; the penalty is set by the spread, Table 9-11). An iteration cap is pyABC's move of closing the generation on the first finishers and discarding latecomers: the paper measures that this understates the barrier's cost (sec. 6.1), and the lane's claim is that in physics it also discards the physics. The paper's domain caveats transfer as well: the barrier's own latency (here, per-iteration kernel launch and compaction when worlds drop out) must be small against one unit of work, and the timing sample must cover the tail. What it does not supply: anything about fidelity, contact, or what a policy exploits.

Same words (straggler, barrier, utilization, asynchronous updates, all-to-all exchange cost, a 4 ms crossover below which coordination beats the barrier), different workload: CPU simulators for Bayesian inference, no agent, no rollout engine, no RL; the predicted-penalty instrument is reusable vocabulary for asynchronous rollout systems, nothing more.

limitations_as_complaints: My barrier-cost prediction has a domain I can only check after the fact: when the collective itself is slow relative to one evaluation (0.3 s per barrier on a 4 ms workload) or when contention at 384 workers gives the asynchronous timing sample a tail the synchronized generations never showed, the prediction fails and I have to mark the configuration as outside the model; three of fifteen configurations were (sec. 5.3, sec. 6.1).

Millions more evaluations do not buy me posterior effective sample size: it stays at 1.9-3.6 times the archive size k because the posterior is reported at the tightest bandwidth the scheduler reached, and on an expensive simulator the schedule never leaves the starting bandwidth epsilon_0 in the hour I have (321x above what the draws supported at epsilon_0 = 10, cell-volume contraction 13% +/- 14%), so the result depends on a hand-set epsilon_0 from prior-predictive draws (sec. 6.4, sec. 7).

Under a wall-clock deadline my completed evaluations over-represent parameter regions with short runtimes; I bound the direct effect at O(W/n) and saw no mean shift on a 1-D Gaussian with coupled runtime, but I do not correct for it and the indirect effect through the adaptive proposal sits in the part of the fidelity ratio I only bound, never measure (sec. 8, Appendix F.5).
